statement: As summarised in a 2007 narrative review of controlled-administration studies, most of them small, often with single doses of low-THC cigarettes or of oral THC given by researchers, many from the author's own laboratory and with participants' sex given for only a few of them (Huestis, 2007; figures second-hand; no systematic search), smoked THC, compared with THC taken by mouth, is associated with THC reaching the blood within minutes rather than hours, with higher and earlier peaks, and after frequent or heavy use THC and its breakdown products remained detectable for days to weeks. Smoked: in 6 people (the review does not give their sex) who smoked single cigarettes of 1.75% and 3.55% THC (about 16 and 34 mg; study conditions), THC appeared in plasma with the first puff, peaked at a mean of 84.3 and 162.2 ng/ml at 9.0 minutes, fell to about 60% and 20% of the peak 15 and 30 minutes after smoking, and was 5 ng/ml or less within 2 hours, staying detectable (at 0.5 ng/ml) for 3 to 12 hours after the lower and 6 to 27 hours after the higher dose; the strongest effects came later, 30 to 45 minutes after smoking began, when blood levels were already falling. How much of the THC in a cigarette reached the blood varied with how people smoked, from 2% to 56% across studies (about 8% to 24% in others, depending strongly on experience with smoking cannabis). By mouth: THC was absorbed more slowly, with lower, later and more irregular peaks; after 20 mg of THC in a chocolate cookie, plasma peaks of 4.4 to 11 ng/ml came 1 to 5 hours after eating, with about 6% of the dose reaching the blood, and a study using a radiolabel method, which the author says overestimated THC, found peaks about 4 to 6 hours after 15 to 20 mg in oil; the review puts oral bioavailability at 4% to 20%, because THC is partly broken down in the stomach and much of it is converted in the liver, among other products into 11-OH-THC, which is active and reaches levels similar to or higher than those of THC after oral intake, against about a tenth of THC after smoking. In the studies described, effects after oral THC began later and lasted longer than after smoking. THC is almost entirely bound to lipoproteins in the blood (95% to 99%) and is stored in body fat; in people who use frequently, its final plasma half-life was about 4.1 days in a study with long sampling (24 to 36 hours in studies with shorter sampling), which the review attributes to storage in and slow release from fat, and THC-COOH, the breakdown product that urine tests measure, had a plasma half-life of up to 12.6 days in one person; the review notes that no pharmacokinetic differences between frequent and occasional use have been substantiated. Plasma: in people who use frequently, low levels remained at least 12 hours after last use (THC 0.86 ng/ml on average in one study; whole-blood levels are about half those in plasma), and after people who used chronically smoked four cigarettes containing labelled THC, a very sensitive method detected it in blood for up to 13 days. Urine: after one smoked cigarette (6 people), the last positive sample for THC-COOH at a cut-off of 15 ng/ml came an average of 33.7 hours (8 to 68.5) after the 1.75% and 88.6 hours (57 to 122.3) after the 3.55% cigarette, with positive and negative samples alternating near the cut-off, while the urine of a person new to cannabis may test negative within a few hours of one cigarette; one person who had used heavily for more than 10 years still tested positive (above 20 ng/ml) 67 days after last use, a case the review calls extreme, and in another person with heavy use cannabinoids were detectable in urine for 93 days (no cut-off given). A positive urine test shows that a person was exposed, not when, how much, by which route or whether they were impaired. These studies predate today's stronger products, edibles, vaporizers and concentrates, gave fixed doses and, where the review gives participants' sex, mostly involved men, so they do not show what happens when people who feel little at first take more. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In small lab studies from before 2007, in which people smoked weak cannabis cigarettes, THC in the blood was highest within minutes of smoking (at about 9 minutes) and fell to low levels within 2 hours, while the felt effects were strongest a little later, at 30 to 45 minutes. When THC was taken by mouth, it entered the blood slowly and at lower levels, peaking 1 to 6 hours later, and the effects began later and lasted longer. THC is stored in body fat and leaves it slowly; in people who use often, it could still be found for days to weeks. After one cigarette, the last positive urine test came about 1 to 4 days later on average, and the urine of someone new to cannabis may test negative within hours; in one person who had used heavily for years, urine was still positive after 67 days, and in another, cannabis could be found for 93 days. A positive test shows use, not when, how much or whether someone was impaired. The studies gave set doses, so they do not show what happens when people who feel little at first take more.
population: People given cannabis or THC in small controlled-administration studies summarised by a 2007 narrative review (6 people, sex not given, in the main smoking and urine studies; 17 volunteers in a capsule study; where the review gives participants' sex, mostly men), and single case reports of heavy long-term use
exposure: Single smoked cigarettes of 1.75% and 3.55% THC (about 16 and 34 mg) or oral THC (20 mg in a cookie; 15 to 20 mg in oil; a 10 mg dronabinol capsule), given by researchers (study conditions only); frequent or heavy long-term use for elimination and detection windows
comparator: Smoking compared with taking THC by mouth; frequent compared with occasional use
outcome: Plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH over time; bioavailability; elimination half-lives; detection windows in plasma and urine
magnitude: Smoked (6 people; sex not given in the review): mean plasma THC peaks 84.3 ng/ml (range 50-129) and 162.2 ng/ml (76-267) at 9.0 minutes; about 60% and 20% of peak at 15 and 30 minutes; 5 ng/ml or less within 2 hours; detectable at 0.5 ng/ml for 3-12 and 6-27 hours; peak effects 30-45 minutes after smoking began; bioavailability 2%-56% (or about 8%-24%). Oral: 20 mg in a cookie, peaks 4.4-11 ng/ml at 1-5 hours, bioavailability about 6%; 15-20 mg in oil, peaks at about 4-6 hours (radiolabel); 10 mg dronabinol (17 volunteers), THC 3.8 ng/ml (1.1-12.7), 11-OH-THC 3.4 (1.2-5.6), THC-COOH 26 (14-46) at 1-2 hours; summary bioavailability 4%-20%; 11-OH-THC about 10% of THC after smoking, similar or higher after oral intake. Elimination: terminal plasma THC half-life about 4.1 days with frequent use (24-36 hours with shorter sampling); THC-COOH plasma half-life up to 12.6 days in one person; no pharmacokinetic difference between frequent and occasional use substantiated; frequent use, plasma THC 0.86 ng/ml at least 12 hours after last use; deuterated THC detectable in blood up to 13 days after four labelled cigarettes (limit 0.02 ng/ml). Urine (6 people, 15 ng/ml cut-off): last positive 33.7 hours (8-68.5) and 88.6 hours (57-122.3) after one cigarette; a person new to cannabis may test negative within a few hours; heavy use, positive up to 67 days (20 ng/ml; one case, called extreme) and cannabinoids detectable for 93 days (no cut-off given) in two individuals.

risk_of_bias.note: The primary studies cannot be appraised from the review, which describes no designs or appraisal; much of the human data come from the author's laboratory, some from conference presentations; early radiolabel methods overestimated THC (card sc_huestis_2007, editors' checklist overall high).

inconsistency.note: The contrast between smoking and eating is consistent across the studies described; the spread of smoked bioavailability (2% to 56%) reflects how people smoked and is reported, not pooled.

indirectness.note: Second-hand (METHODS §6.3), and the products and people differ from today's: low-THC cigarettes and single doses, participants' sex mostly not given (men where it is), little on daily use, nothing on vaporizers, concentrates or commercial edibles.

imprecision.note: Tiny samples (6 people in the main smoking and urine studies) with large differences between people; the weeks-long urine windows rest on single cases.

grade.reasoning: The cited human studies gave known doses under controlled conditions, and such evidence starts high (as for the methamphetamine pharmacokinetic claims); seen only through a narrative review, it is rated down one level each for risk of bias (not appraisable, much from one laboratory), indirectness (second-hand, old products) and imprecision: very low. Starting low instead, because the review does not describe how the studies were designed, gives the same result. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3). Status replicated: the review describes the same contrast between smoking and eating from several groups (for example Ohlsson et al., 1980; Wall et al., 1983; Huestis et al., 1992), although the urine detection windows come from single studies and cases.
